title: Firearm case reveals new details in fatal Toronto police shooting
subtitle: A judge named the two Toronto police officers who shot Kwasi Skene-Peters during a firefight outside downtown club.
article: A court case has provided new information, including video footage, related to the Toronto police shooting death of Kwasi Skene-Peters in 2015 - material that would likely not have otherwise been made public until the coroner's inquest into his death.
Skene-Peters, 21, was killed in a firefight in the early morning of July 25, 2015 in Toronto's Entertainment District.

Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), cleared two unnamed subject officers of criminal wrongdoing, saying Skene-Peters fired at the officers first through the windshield of his car in a parking lot.
Neither officer spoke to the SIU or provided a copy of their notes, as is their legal right.
Accounts of the shooting from the officers form part of a ruling released last month convicting the man in the passenger seat of Skene-Peters' car, Kevin Duro, of firearm-related offences.

Superior Court Justice Robert Goldstein's judgment was released just days before the coroner's office announced earlier this month that an inquest will be held into Skene-Peters' death, although no date has been set.
The ruling identifies two officers as having shot at Skene-Peters: Const. Jeffery Riel and Const. Darryl Lambie.
An SIU spokesman would not confirm with the Star that Riel and Lambie are the subject officers, citing privacy legislation. The officers declined to comment through a Toronto police spokesperson.

According to the SIU, Toronto police had received information that Skene-Peters would be at Tryst nightclub the night of July 24, 2015 and would be armed and dangerous. He was the subject of a Canada-wide warrant for the double murder of Mohamed Abdiwal Dirie and Abdiwel Abdullah.
A number of officers initiated a takedown of Skene-Peters around 3 a.m. when he returned to his car from the club, after having already been under police surveillance, the SIU said.

Three officers from the now-disbanded Toronto Anti-Violence Intervention Strategy (TAVIS), two of whom the SIU said are the subject officers, approached the front of Skene-Peters' car with their guns drawn shouting police challenges.

"As the officers continued to shout, a firefight erupted," according to an SIU news release. "It lasted approximately four seconds. It was during this exchange of gunfire that Mr. Skene-Peters sustained a single, fatal gunshot wound to the chest."

SIU director Tony Loparco concluded that, based on the accounts of "multiple witnesses," Skene-Peters fired two shots at the officers while they were shouting commands, and that the two subject officers returned fire "multiple times."

The SIU said police discovered Skene-Peters' wound after he managed to flee from his car and tripped over a man who had fallen on the ground. A black semi-automatic handgun flew from his hand and landed at the feet of an officer.
Duro, 26, who was sitting in the passenger seat, fled and was arrested in the parking lot. In the ruling convicting him, the judge summarizes the testimony of the officers leading up to the shooting.
"When takedown was called the three (TAVIS) officers ran from the alley towards the Ford Focus. Const. Riel saw two people in the front of the car," Goldstein wrote.

"He pointed his gun at them and yelled words to the effect of 'police, hands up, don't move.' He then saw a muzzle flash and heard bullets snapping. He realized that someone was shooting at him through the front window of the Ford Focus. He returned fire."
Riel said he then moved to hide behind a truck and saw a person crawling from underneath, who turned out to be Duro.
"Const. Lambie testified that he also ran up to the Ford Focus and pointed his gun. He yelled commands. He ordered the occupants to get out of the car and show their hands," Goldstein wrote.
"The driver reversed into the wall of Tryst nightclub. Const. Lambie then realized that the driver was shooting at police through the windshield. He shot back."
According to Goldstein's ruling, the dashboard camera from a police cruiser in the parking lot "captured much of the action." The SIU took control of the scene at 6:25 a.m.
Duro's case is back in court Nov. 28.
